<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|brazen|667|breach}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|With ''brazen'' din blast you the city’s ear.
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iv. 8.}}}}
'''3.''' Extremely strong; impenetrable: from brass often serving as a type of strength, impenetrability, and the like: as, “environed with a ''brazen'' wall,” ''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 4.—'''4.''' Impudent; having a front like brass.
{{smaller block|Such a ''brazen'' dog sure never my eyes beheld.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', She Stoops to Conquer, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Talbot . . . appeared daily with ''brazen'' front before the princess whose ruin he had plotted.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi.}}}}
Also spelled ''brasen''.

{{smaller|'''Brazen age.''' See ''ages in mythology and history'', under ''age''.—'''Brazen dish''', a brass dish made in the time of Henry VIII., and kept chained to a pillar at Wirksworth in Derbyshire, England. It is used by the lead-miners in the Low Peak as a standard measure.—'''Brazen horn.''' Same as ''burghmote-horn''.—'''Brazen sea''' (2 Ki. xxv. 13), in ''Jewish antiq.'', a large vessel of brass placed in Solomon’s temple, called a ''molten sea'' in 1 Ki. vii. 23–25, where it is described. It stood on 12 brazen oxen, and was 10 cubits from brim to brim, 5 in height, and 30 in circumference. It was designed for the priests to wash themselves in before they performed the service of the temple.}}

'''brazen''' (brā′zn), ''v. t.''   [< ''brazen'', ''a.'']   To behave with insolence or effrontery in regard to: with an indefinite ''it'' as object.
{{smaller block|Men would face it and ''brazen it.''{{right|''Latimer.''}}}}
{{smaller|'''To brazen out''', to persevere in treating with effrontery: with an indefinite ''it'', or a noun like ''matter'', ''affair'', ''business'', etc.}}
{{smaller block|I’m resolved to ''brazen'' the ''business out.''
{{right|''Sir J. Vanbrugh'', The Relapse, iv. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thornton . . . ''brazened it out'' with his usual impudence.
{{right|''Bulwer'', Pelham, lxxviii.}}}}

'''brazen-browed''' (brā′zn-broud), ''a.'' Shameless; impudent.

{{smaller block|Noon-day vices and ''brazen-browed'' iniquities.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Christ. Mor., i. 35.}}}}

'''brazen-face''' (brā′zn-fās), ''n.'' An impudent person; one remarkable for effrontery.
{{smaller block|Well said, ''brazen-face'' ; hold it out.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iv. 2.}}}}

'''brazen-faced''' (brā′zn-fāst), ''a.'' Impudent; bold to excess; shameless: as, “a ''brazen-faced'' varlet,” ''Shak.'', Lear, ii. 2.

'''brazen-fisted''' (brā′zn-fis″ted), ''a.'' Having hard fists, as if of brass.

'''brazenly''' (brā′zn-li), ''adv.'' In a brazen manner; boldly; impudently.

'''brazenness''' (brā′zn-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' Appearance like brass; brassiness.—'''2.''' Impudence; excess of assurance.
{{smaller block|He had a sonorous bass voice, and an air of self-confidence inclining to ''brazenness.''
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, ii. 1.}}}}

'''brazier<sup>1</sup>''' (brā′ziėr), ''n.''   [Also ''brasier;'' < ME. ''brasiere'', ''brasyere'', a worker in brass, < ''bras'', brass, + ''-i-ere'', ''-y-ere'', as in ''collier'', etc. Cf. ''braze''<sup>1</sup>.]   An artificer who works in brass.

'''brazier<sup>2</sup>''' (brā′ziėr), ''n.''   [Also ''brasier;'' < F. ''brasier'', a pan of live coals, formerly ''bracier'', “a burning coal, quickfire of coals, hot embers” (Cotgrave) (cf. ''braisière'', a camp-kettle), < ''braise'', live coals: see ''braize''<sup>1</sup>.]   An open pan for burning charcoal, used especially for heating rooms in southern and eastern countries, such as Italy, China, Japan, etc.
{{smaller block|Four nice-looking Japanese girls brought us thick cotton quilts to sit upon, and ''braziers'' full of burning charcoal, to warm ourselves by.
{{right|''Lady Brassey'', Voyage of Sunbeam, II. xix.}}}}

[[File:century v01 p0693 c1f1.png|center|289px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Bronze Brazier made in 1675 by Pedro Cerdanyæ for the Guildhall of Barcelona. (From “L’Art pour Tous.”)}}}}

'''brazier'''<sup>3</sup> (brā′z̮iėr), ''n.''   [Another form of ''braize''<sup>2</sup>, D. ''brasem'', etc., bream: see ''bream''<sup>1</sup>.]   A name used on the northern coast of Ireland for the common sea-bream, ''Pagellus centrodontus''.

'''brazil''' (bra-zil′), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''brasil'' (with accent on the first syllable; cf. ''brassil'', ''brissel-cock''), < ME. ''brasil'', ''brasyle'' = ODan. ''brasilie'', Dan. ''brasilie''(''-træ'') = Norw. ''bresel'', ''brisel'', < OF. ''bresil'', mod. F. ''brésil'' = Pr. ''bresil'', ''brezilh'' = Sp. OPg. ''brasil'' (> mod. It. ''brasile'': ML. ''brasilium'', ''braxile'', ''bresillum'', ''brisillum'', ''brisiacum''), orig. a red dyewood brought from the East. Origin uncertain; perhaps, as Diez suggests, < Pr. ''brezilhar'' (= F. ''brésiller''), break into fragments, crumble, < ''briza'', a fragment, little ly fragments, rubbish: see ''briss''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'', ''breeze''<sup>3</sup>), < ''brizar'' = F. ''briser'', break: see ''bruise'' and ''debris''. The name would refer to the form in which the dyewood was imported. Now usually in comp. ''brazil-wood'', with direct reference to the country Brazil. The country, named ''Santa Cruz'' by its (second) discoverer, Pedro Alvarez Cabral (1500), afterward received the name ''Brazil'', it is said, from King Emmanuel of Portugal, on account of its producing red dyewood. The name had been long before applied to a supposed island in the Atlantic, perhaps by association with Pliny’s ''Insulæ Purpurariæ'' (lit. Purple Islands), sometimes supposed to refer to Madeira and Porto Santo.]   '''1†.''' A heavy dyewood of the genus ''Cæsalpinia'' (''C. Sappan''), imported from the East, now known as ''sappan-wood'' (which see).
{{smaller block|<poem>Him nedeth not his colour for to dien
With ''brasil'' ne with grain of Portingale.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', C. T. (ed. Tyrwhitt), l. 15464.}}}}
'''2.''' A very heavy dyewood, from Brazil and other parts of tropical America. {{smaller|The true brazilwood is from the leguminous tree ''Cæsalpinia echinata'', but the name is also given to ''C. peltophoroides''. Woods known as peach-wood and lima-wood are said to be from the same species. The wood has a slightly aromatic odor and a bitter-sweet taste. To extract the coloring matter, the wood is finely ground, allowed to ferment in the air, and then boiled in copper cylinders with water. The extract produces purple dyes with salts of iron, and red with salts of alumina. Lakes used by decorators are also made from it, and common red ink is prepared by adding a little alum and acid to a decoction of it. Also spelled ''brasil''.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Are my bones ''brazil'', or my flesh of oak?
O, mend what thou hast made, what I have broke.</poem> {{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, iii. 5.}}}}
'''3.''' Sulphate of iron. [North. Eng.]

'''brazil-cock†''', ''n.''   [Also written ''brasil-cock'', and corruptly ''brissel-cock'', ''brissil-cock'', with ref. to Brazil, representing America, the place of its origin.]   A turkey.

'''braziletto''' (braz-i-let′ō), ''n.''   [Pg. ''brazilete'', brazil-wood; Sp. ''brasilete'', F. ''brésillet'', dim. of ''brasil'', etc.: see ''brazil''.]   A wood resembling brazil-wood, obtained from the West Indies and parts of Central America, from species of ''Cæsalpinia'', ''C. crista'' and ''C. pectinata'', and the nearly allied ''Peltophorum Linnæi''. {{smaller|It is used for dyeing and in cabinet-work. The ''bastard'' or ''false braziletto'' of the same region includes a number of different shrubs or trees, as ''Picramnia Antidesma'', natural order ''Simarubaceæ'', the saxifragaceous ''Weinmannia pinnata'', and the araliaceous ''Sciadophyllum capitatum''.}}

'''Brazilian''' (brạ-zil′ian), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.''   [< ''Brazil'' (Pg. ''Brazil'', Sp. ''Brasil'', etc.: see ''brazil'') + ''-ian''.]   Pertaining to Brazil, an empire and the largest country of South America: as, ''Brazilian'' productions.—{{smaller|'''Brazilian balsam.''' See ''balsam''.—'''Brazilian bean.''' See ''bean''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Brazilian cocoa''', guarana.—'''Brazilian pebbles''', lenses for spectacles ground from pure, colorless rock-crystal obtained from Brazil.—'''Brazilian plait''', in England, plait made of dried flag-grass which is imported from the West Indies, and perhaps from South America.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A native or an inhabitant of Brazil.

'''brazilin, braziline''' (braz′i-lin), ''n.''   [< ''brazil'' + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>, ''-ine''<sup>2</sup>; also written ''breziline'', after F. ''brésiline''.]   A crystallizable coloring principle (C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>5</sub>) obtained from brazil-wood. Also written ''brasilin'', ''brasiline'', ''breziline''.

'''Brazil-nut''' (bra̤-zil′nut), ''n.'' The seed of the fruit of ''Bertholletia excelsa'', a tree of the natural order ''Myrtaceæ'', a native of Guiana, Venezuela, and Brazil. {{smaller|The fruit is nearly round and about 6 inches in diameter, having an extremely hard shell about ½ inch thick, and containing from 18 to 24}}
{{smaller|triangular wrinkled seeds, which are so fitted together within the shell that when once disturbed it is impossible to replace them. When the fruits are ripe they fall from the tree and are collected by Indians. They are then split open with an ax, and the seeds are taken out and packed in baskets for transportation. Besides being used as an article of dessert, a bland oil, used by watchmakers and others, is expressed from them. See ''Bertholletia''.}}

[[File:century v01 p0693 c2f1.png|center|289px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Brazil-nut.}}}}
{{c|{{smaller|''a'', fruit of ''Bertholletia excelsa'' ; ''b'', same with portion of shell removed ; ''c'', a single nut on larger scale.}}}}

'''Brazil-root''' (bra̤-zil′röt), ''n.'' A name sometimes given to the root of ipecacuanha.

'''Brazil tea.''' Same as ''maté''.

'''Brazil wax.''' See ''wax''.

'''brazil-wood''' (bra̤-zil′wu̇d), ''n.'' Same as ''brazil.'' with broad flat jaws, used in brazing. See ''braze''<sup>2</sup>.

'''breach''' (brēch), ''n.''   [< (1) ME. ''breche'', also, without assibilation, ''breke'' (> mod. E. ''break'', ''n.'', and dial. ''breek''<sup>2</sup>, q. v.), also ''brekke'' (> mod. E. dial. ''breck'', q. v.), < AS. *''brece'', *''gebrece'', found only in the sense of ‘a piece’ (in comp. ''brec-mǣlum'', piecemeal, ''hlāf-gebrece'', a piece of bread), = OFries. ''breke'', ''bretse'', ''breze'', ''bresze'', ''breszie'', m. and f., a break, breach, fracture, = MD. ''breke'', a break, breach, fracture, = MLG. ''breke'', a breach, violation; the above forms being mixed with (2) ME. ''bruche'', *''bryche'', also, without assibilation, ''bryke'', ''brike'', a breach, violation, injury, ruin (> E. dial. ''brick''<sup>1</sup>, a flaw, Sc. ''brick'', a breach, a division of land), < AS. ''bryce'', ''brice'' (= OHG. ''bruh'', MHG. G. ''bruch''), m., a breaking, breach, fracture, violation, fragment, piece (cf. MD. ''breucke'', D. ''breuk'', f., a breaking, fracture, rupture, crime, fine, = G. ''brüche'', f., a crime, fine); cf. (3) E. dial. ''brock'', AS. ''gebroc'', neut., = D. ''brok'', m., = OHG. ''brocco'', MHG. ''brocke'', G. ''brocke'', ''brocken'', m., = Goth. ''gabruka'', f., a fragment, piece, bit (see ''brock''<sup>2</sup>); and (4) several other closely related noun forms (see ''brack''<sup>1</sup>, ''brake''<sup>1</sup>, etc.); < ''brecan'' (pret. ''bræc'', pp. ''brocen''), break. ''Breach'' is thus a deriv. of ''break'', related, in present though not in orig. form, to ''break'' as ''speech'' is to ''speak''. Hence (from ME. or MLG.) OF. MF. ''breche'', ''bresche'', mod. F. ''brèche'', a breach, gap, break, injury, > Sp. Pg. ''brecha'', a breach, = It. ''breccia'', formerly also ''brecchia'', a breach, a gap, a rupture, = G. ''bresche'', a breach in a wall, etc. The It. ''breccia'', gravel, now technically breccia, = F. ''brèche'', breccia, is closely related, but may be taken from the G.: see ''breccia''. See ''break'', ''n.'', ''breek''<sup>2</sup>, ''breck'', ''brick''<sup>1</sup>, ''brack''<sup>1</sup>, ''brake''<sup>3</sup>, related to and in part identical with ''breach''; see also ''brick''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' The act of breaking: now used only figuratively of the violation or neglect of a law, contract, or any other obligation, or of a custom.
{{smaller block|<poem>A custom
More honour’d in the ''breach'' than the observance.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The deadliest sin her mind could reach
Was of monastic rule the ''breach''.</poem>{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, ii. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' An opening made by breaking down a portion of a solid body, as a wall, a dike, or a river-bank; a rupture; a break; a gap.
{{smaller block|<poem>Could make old Trent,
Drunk with my sorrow, to start out in ''breaches'',
To drown their herds, their cattle, and their corn.</poem>{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sad Shepherd, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thou hast made the earth to tremble; thou hast broken it; heal the ''breaches'' thereof. {{right|Ps. lx. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|He then led his men to the assault, taking charge himself of those who were to storm the ''breach''.{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 11.}}}}
'''3†.''' A break or interruption in utterance.
{{smaller block|<poem>And all her sister Nymphes with one consent
Supplide her sobbing ''breaches'' with sad complement.</poem>{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. iv. 35.}}}}
'''4.''' A rupture of friendly relations; difference; quarrel.
{{smaller block|<poem>There’s fallen between him and my lord
An unkind ''breach''.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iv. 1.}}}}
'''5.''' Infraction; violation; infringement: as, a ''breach'' of the peace, of a promise, or of a contract.
{{smaller block|This ''breach'' upon kingly power was without precedent.
{{right|''Clarendon.''}}}}
{{smaller block|It is no ''breach'' of charity to call these fools.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Religio Medici, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The first steps in the ''breach'' of a man’s integrity are much more important than men are aware of.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 448.}}}}
'''6.''' Injury; wound; bruise.
{{smaller block|''Breach'' for ''breach'', eye for eye, tooth for tooth.
{{right|Lev. xxiv. 20.}}}}
'''7.''' The breaking of waves; the dashing of surf.
{{smaller block|Some hour before you took me from the ''breach'' of the sea was my sister drowned.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|We scudded with frightful velocity before the sea, and the water made clear ''breaches'' over us.
{{right|''Poe'', Tales, I. 154.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Breach of arrest,''' a military offense committed by an officer in arrest who leaves his quarters or limits without authority from his superior officer. It is punishable by cashiering.—'''Breach of arrestment,''' in ''Scots law'', an act of contempt of legal authority committed by an arrestee disregarding the arrestment used in his hands, and paying the sum or delivering the goods arrested to the common debtor.—'''Breach of close,''' in ''law'', an unwarrantable entry on another’s land.—'''Breach of covenant,''' a violation of a covenant contained in a deed either to do or refrain from doing a direct act.—'''Breach of duty,''' the failure to execute any office, employment, trust, etc., in a proper manner.—'''Breach of promise,''' a violation of one’s word or undertaking; non-fulfilment of what one had agreed to do: often used absolutely for breach of promise of marriage.—'''Breach of the peace,''' a violation of the public}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
